title: Password Managers and Passkeys in 2026: A Simple Guide to Staying Safe
seoTitle: Password Managers and Passkeys in 2026: A Simple Guide
excerpt: Password managers and passkeys explained: how they work, free vs paid options with 2026 prices, step-by-step setup, 2FA basics and mistakes to avoid.
content:
Quick answer: A password manager is an encrypted vault that creates a different strong password for every account and fills it in for you, so the only one you have to remember is your master password. A passkey goes a step further: it replaces the password with a cryptographic key pair stored on your phone, computer or security key, and you unlock it with your fingerprint, face or PIN. Passkeys can't be phished the way passwords can. As of November 2026, the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) recommends using passkeys wherever a site offers them, plus a password manager and two-step verification everywhere else.

Most people cope with too many accounts by reusing one or two favorite passwords. Attackers count on that: when one site leaks your password, they try it on your email and bank next. This guide covers the two tools that fix the problem, what they cost as of November 13, 2026, and how to set them up in an afternoon.

What is a password manager and how does it work?

A password manager is an app (often with a browser extension) that stores your logins in an encrypted vault and syncs them across your devices. The NCSC's guide to password managers lists the features to expect: it generates a strong, unique password for each account, autofills it when you log in, syncs across devices, and warns you when a saved password shows up in a breach.

The security rests on one idea: your vault is encrypted on your device before it is uploaded anywhere. Bitwarden's published security whitepaper is one example of how this works. Your master password is run through a key derivation function (PBKDF2 with 600,000 rounds by default, or Argon2id if you switch) to produce the key that unlocks your vault. Vault data is encrypted with AES 256-bit encryption, all of it happens locally, and the master password itself is never sent to Bitwarden's servers. The company says it cannot read your data.

The catch is that your master password really matters. Bitwarden is blunt: forget it and you are locked out unless you set up emergency access or account recovery in advance. Pick a long passphrase you will remember, and protect the manager with two-step verification, as the NCSC recommends.

There is a phishing benefit too. The NCSC notes that a manager only autofills on the correct website, so it won't fill your bank password into a lookalike page. If autofill suddenly doesn't work, check the web address before typing anything.

Which password managers are free, and which are worth paying for?

You may already have one. The NCSC says saving passwords in the browser or operating system on your own devices is safe and easiest if you stick to one ecosystem. A third-party manager earns its keep when you mix, say, an iPhone with a Windows laptop.

What is a passkey, and why is it safer than a password?

A passkey is a sign-in credential built on the FIDO Alliance's FIDO2 standards, WebAuthn and CTAP. Apple's support page about passkey security explains how it works: your device creates a unique key pair for each account. The public key goes to the website and isn't secret. The private key stays with you, and the server never learns it. To sign in, you approve with whatever unlocks your device, such as a fingerprint, face scan or PIN.

That is why passkeys resist phishing: there is no password to type into a fake page and nothing reusable for a breach to leak. The FIDO Alliance says a passkey on its own is more secure than a password plus a one-time code, because those codes and phone approval prompts can still be phished. The NCSC reached a similar conclusion in its technical paper and now recommends passkeys over passwords wherever they are available.

Passkeys come in two kinds. Synced passkeys are backed up across your devices by a credential manager such as Apple Passwords, Google Password Manager or a third-party app. Device-bound passkeys stay on one device, such as a hardware security key, which the FIDO Alliance rates as the highest-assurance option.

Which big services support passkeys?

As of November 2026, the FIDO Alliance says passkeys work in all major operating systems and browsers and with third-party passkey providers. A few examples you can set up today, each documented on the company's own help pages:

  • Google accounts. Supported on Windows 10, macOS Ventura, ChromeOS 109 or later, Android 9 or iOS 16 or later, in Chrome 109, Safari 16, Edge 109 and Firefox 122 or newer.
  • Apple. Passkeys are stored in the Passwords app and synced through iCloud Keychain, which Apple says is end-to-end encrypted.
  • Microsoft accounts. Personal and work or school accounts can sign in with a passkey saved to a device, a security key or a synced credential manager.
  • Password managers. Bitwarden, Proton Pass and 1Password all list passkey storage on their plans.

For other sites, the NCSC suggests checking each account's security settings and watching for prompts to upgrade to a passkey.

How do you set up a password manager?

  1. Choose one. Built-in is fine inside one ecosystem; pick a third-party app if you mix platforms.
  2. Create a strong master password. NIST's current guidance (SP 800-63B, Revision 4) says passwords used on their own should be at least 15 characters, and that services shouldn't force you to mix in symbols and numbers. A passphrase of several unrelated words is easier to remember. CISA suggests 5 to 7 random words.
  3. Turn on two-step verification for the manager itself, and save any recovery code it gives you somewhere safe offline.
  4. Import your passwords from your browser, then install the extension and phone app.
  5. Fix the worst passwords first. Use the manager's health or security report to replace reused and breached passwords, starting with email and banking.

How do you create your first passkey?

Your email account is a sensible place to start, since password reset links for other accounts usually go there. Using a Google account as the example, from Google's help page:

  1. Make sure your phone or computer has a screen lock turned on.
  2. Go to myaccount.google.com/signinoptions/passkeys and sign in.
  3. Tap Create a passkey, then confirm with your fingerprint, face or PIN.
  4. Repeat on your other devices if you want, or let your credential manager sync it.

For a Microsoft personal account, go to account.live.com/proofs/manage, choose Add a new way to sign in or verify, then Face, Fingerprint, PIN, or Security Key. Google notes that adding a passkey doesn't remove your password or recovery options, so you keep a fallback.

What should you know about two-factor authentication?

Two-factor authentication (2FA), also called two-step verification (2SV) or multi-factor authentication (MFA), asks for a second proof after your password. The NCSC calls turning it on the first and most important step, because it protects you even if your password is phished or leaked.

Not all second factors are equal, though any of them beats a password alone:

  • Text message (SMS) codes. Common, but NIST lists attacks where criminals convince a mobile carrier to redirect your number and receive the code.
  • Authenticator app codes. Short-lived codes generated on your phone. They don't depend on your number, but can still be typed into a fake site.
  • Push approvals. Convenient, but NIST warns about authentication fatigue, where attackers send prompt after prompt until someone taps Approve to make them stop.
  • Passkeys and security keys. Phishing resistant by design. Google notes that when your account has 2-Step Verification, signing in with a passkey covers the second step, since it proves you have your device.

The same weakness applies to one-time codes from your bank or mobile carrier: whoever gets the code can use it. If someone calls or messages asking you to read out a code you didn't request, hang up and contact the company through its official app or website.

What are the most common mistakes?

  • Reusing passwords. One breach can then open several accounts, which is the problem the NCSC says a password manager solves.
  • Saving passwords or passkeys on a shared computer. The NCSC says never save passwords on a public or shared device, and Google warns that anyone who can unlock a device holding your passkey can get into your account.
  • Losing the keys to the vault. Write down recovery codes when you turn on 2FA and set up emergency access or a recovery contact if your manager offers one.
  • Approving a sign-in you didn't start. If a push prompt or code arrives out of nowhere, deny it and change that account's password.
  • Changing passwords on a schedule for no reason. NIST's guidance tells services not to force periodic changes; change a password when there is evidence it was compromised.

FAQ

Is it safe to keep all my passwords in one place?

For most people, yes. A good manager encrypts your vault on your device, so the provider can't read it. The risk moves to your master password, which is why a long passphrase and two-step verification matter.

Do passkeys replace password managers?

Not yet. Passkeys are stored in a credential manager, which is the same app that holds your passwords, and many sites still only support passwords. As of November 2026, the NCSC's advice is passkeys where offered and strong unique passwords plus 2SV everywhere else.

What happens to my passkeys if I lose my phone?

If they are synced passkeys, they are backed up by your credential manager and come back when you sign in on a new device. Remove the lost device's passkey from your account settings, which Google's help page explains how to do. Device-bound passkeys on a lost security key are gone, so register a backup key.

Is the free Bitwarden or Proton Pass plan enough?

For storing and autofilling passwords on all your devices, both free plans cover the basics as of November 13, 2026. Paid tiers add extras such as a built-in authenticator, file attachments and emergency access.

Can someone steal my fingerprint through a passkey?

No. According to the FIDO Alliance, biometric data stays on your device and is never sent to the website. The site only receives confirmation that the check passed.
